findings.sentence: *Three months of cramming four authors into one writing skill, and the delete that finally made it sound like me.*
I was on the ferry home re-reading *Dharma Bums* when I got the idea that cost me three months.

Kerouac keeps a sentence going well past the point where a normal sentence gives up, and by the time he finally lets go of you he's punched you in the face four or five times to make sure the thing landed.
So the thought arrived on its own.
I researched and synthesized four writers I love.
I broke each one down into mechanics, crammed all four into a single writing skill, and pointed it at everything I put words into.
Essays, documents, social posts, anything that deserved better than the usual AI slop.
The essays kept routing to Sedaris.
That part actually made sense, because comedic deflation is how I tend to write anyway.
Every punchline it built landed on my mother and my sisters.
It gets better.
I'd be three paragraphs deep into agentic workflows, mid technical explanation, and the thing would button the whole essay on a warm little callback to hanging out with my Mom.
Sedaris writes about his family, I asked for Sedaris, and it handed me a family.
The other three didn't save me either.
Kerouac gave me the length and none of the effect, so the sentence would run on and on and never get around to the part where it hits you.
A model can take a writer apart and show you every gear in the machine.
It can't hand you the reason the guy sat down to write it.
I kept at it anyway for about three months.
First I tried the half measure, which is what everybody tries.
Keep a few of the tendencies, hold onto the good parts, sand the rest off.
Turns out the good parts come with the bad ones stapled to the back, and it kept popping up in the worst possible spots.
So I brought in the skill chain, injected more rules, fed it my own writing, and started scrubbing the authors out.

I had Claude write me exercises to get more of me and less of them, and the four of them were still surfacing here and there, which is when I gave up on the surgery and went over to Alex Lieberman's content machine approach.
The fix was the delete key.
I pulled all four of them out completely, kept every word I'd written myself, and started fresh.
A few weeks ago OpenAI quietly stopped ChatGPT from writing in the style of named authors, living or dead.
It's a legal move, copyright suits, lawyers doing lawyer things.
The sanctioned workaround is that you can still describe the techniques, you just can't name the writer.
No matter how hard you push a model to copy somebody's style and drop it into your own work, it won't feel right putting it out there in the world.
So the job flipped.
I don't ask it to sound like anyone now.
I brain dump an idea into Claude, have it invoke the /creative-partner skill, and let it grill me on the pile I just spewed into it.
It reads the whole mess and starts asking questions to make the idea coherent.
It tells me where I could expand, where I might want to pivot, and pushes me in a few directions I wouldn't have gone on my own.
Then it hands the final call back to me, every single time.
Four writers I love couldn't get me to sound like myself.
Nobody's brought up my sisters since.

I was on the ferry home, re-reading Dharma Bums, watching Kerouac keep a single sentence going long enough to punch me in the face four or five separate times before he let it stop.
Around that same stretch I'd found Nate B.
Jones on YouTube, who has a pile of episodes about teaching an LLM your personal taste.
Those two things met somewhere in the middle of the harbor and turned into a thought.
I picked four.
I researched each one, synthesized how they build a sentence, broke their moves down into mechanics, and crammed all four into a single writing skill.
From then on, every essay, every document, every social post would come out the other end sounding like it had been raised by better parents than the usual AI slop.
It leaned Sedaris for the essays, and honestly, that tracked.
Comedic deflation is how I tend to write anyway, so of course that's the door it walked through.
What didn't track was where the deflation landed.
The punch lines kept coming back aimed at my mother and my sisters.
So there I'd sit, reading a piece about agentic workflows that closed on a warm little callback to hanging out with my Mom.
I couldn't repeat the exact line to you if you held a gun to my head.
The other three didn't do any better.
Kerouac gave me the length with none of the effect, the sentence rolling on and on and arriving nowhere in particular.
None of that is the model doing a bad job.
It can read any of those four and hand you a clean breakdown of how the engine turns over.
What it can't hand you is the soul underneath.
So everything it produced felt foreign and cringy, not because the prose was broken, but because it sounded like nothing that had ever come out of me.
Naturally, I did the thing anybody does after sinking real time into something that isn't working.
Trim the authors back, hold onto their better tendencies, leave the rest.
They kept popping up in the worst possible ways, like a guy you fired who still shows up to the office holiday party.
I was looking into starting a Substack, and everything the machine was handing me was too cringy to publish and had nothing to do with me or anything I'd actually lived.
So I brought in the skill chain, injected more rules, fed it my own writing, and started scrubbing the authors out.
I had Claude write me exercises designed to pull more of me out and leave less of them in, and they still snuck through the cracks.
Three months in, I deleted all four of them.
Kept every word I'd written myself.
A few weeks ago, OpenAI quietly stopped ChatGPT from writing in the style of named authors, living or dead.
It's a legal move, copyright suits.
The sanctioned workaround is that you can still describe the techniques, you just can't say whose they are.
Not because of the workaround.
Because no matter how hard you push a model to copy somebody's style and bolt it onto your own work, it won't feel right putting it out into the world.
I ran that experiment on my own time for three months and landed on the same policy, minus the lawyers.
You start off copying whoever you love, and if you keep typing long enough, all of those influences slowly meld into one voice that only you could have come up with.
There's no version where you hand it four writers' mechanics and get yourself back.
So the job changed.
I stopped asking it to write like anybody.
Now I brain dump an idea into Claude, invoke the creative-partner skill, and let it grill me on the pile I just spewed in.
It asks questions until the idea holds together, points at where it could expand, points at where I might want to pivot instead, and it does that across multiple rounds.
Then it hands the decision back to me.
The most it could ever do was keep asking where mine was.
Four authors, three months, one delete key.

findings.sentence: *I spent three months teaching a machine to sound like my favorite writers.
Then I deleted them.*
I was commuting home on the Staten Island ferry, rereading *Dharma Bums*, when I started admiring the way Jack Kerouac could keep a sentence moving long after a normal person would've pulled over.
It didn't end so much as wind up and punch you again.
Jones talking on YouTube about teaching LLMs your personal taste.
My brain smashed the two things together.
That question looked harmless.
So does a loose floorboard.
I went down the rabbit hole and started researching four of my favorite writers.
I broke down how they worked, synthesized the findings, and stuffed all four into one writing skill like a literary turducken I expected to introduce itself as me.
The model understood the mechanics.
It could keep a Kerouac sentence shambling across the page, but the sentence wasn't hitting anything.
It just refused to sit down.
Vonnegut came back sounding like a children's book drifting through outer space.
Thompson acted like somebody hooked a caffeine bag straight into my veins at 2 a.m.
while every agent in the terminal formed a cheer squad.
Sedaris was the most persistent.
Unfortunately, it also picked up his family material and started generating punchlines about my mother and sisters.
Somehow, an essay about agentic workflows would wander away from the technical point and end with me hanging out with Mom.
My imaginary sisters were apparently busy that day.
Mercifully, I can't remember the exact punchline.
I only remember the feeling of reading it and watching a stranger wearing my clothes walk into the room.
The model had reverse-engineered another writer so thoroughly that it invented a childhood for me.
The annoying part was that Claude wasn't doing a bad job.
It followed my instructions.
I asked for Kerouac, Thompson, Sedaris, and Vonnegut, and it marched all four of them onto the page wearing little name tags.
I just didn't belong in the group photo.
I kept tinkering for about three months.
When I started looking into launching a Substack, the problem became harder to ignore.
The jokes walked into the room wearing a tiny bow tie and waited for applause.
So I added more rules.
I fed it my own work and had Claude give me writing exercises so I could get more of myself into the mix.
Then I tried negotiating with the authors.
That half measure lasted until those tendencies started popping up in the worst places again.
Apparently, an author mode is like glitter.
You don't keep a tasteful amount.
You find it in your socks three weeks later.
I finally removed all four of them, kept everything I'd written, and started fresh.
When bits of the old approach still crept through, I turned to Alex Lieberman's content machine approach and changed the job entirely.
A few weeks ago, OpenAI quietly stopped ChatGPT from writing in the style of named authors, living or dead.
You can still describe the techniques.
You just can't name the writer.
That might solve a naming problem.
It doesn't solve the writing problem.
You can remove Kerouac's name and ask for a long sentence that flows through multiple beats.
That doesn't mean you'll feel the punch.
You can request comedic deflation without mentioning Sedaris.
The machine may still send your fictional sisters over to finish the joke.
Give a model enough measurements and it'll try to solve a voice like an equation.
Sentence length plus comedic deflation plus cosmic children's narrator plus caffeine poisoning.
The math can balance and the answer can still sound nothing like you.
Good writing doesn't come from knowing how many commas somebody uses.
It comes from time, lived experience, and those sleepless nights when something is clawing around inside you and the only way to get it out is through the keyboard.
Most writers start by copying the people they love.
You keep typing and those influences slowly melt together with everything that's happened to you.
Eventually, the seams disappear and you're left with a voice nobody else could've assembled.
Now I brain-dump the idea into Claude and have the creative-partner skill grill me.
It asks questions, pushes me through multiple rounds, and shows me places where the idea could expand or pivot.
That's still mine.
What I needed was a creative partner willing to sit across from me and keep asking questions until I sounded like myself.
If a sister shows up, she gets cut.

findings.sentence: # I Built a Writing Skill and Then Deleted the Writers
The problem was that it sounded like everyone except me.

I was commuting home on the Staten Island ferry, re-reading *Dharma Bums*, when I had one of those ideas that feels brilliant for about eight seconds before it starts chewing through your free time like a raccoon in a garbage bag.
I was paying attention to the way Kerouac keeps a sentence moving.
The thing just rolls and rolls until it verbally punches you in the face multiple times, somehow without stopping to ask if you’re okay.
Jones’ YouTube channel.
He had multiple episodes about teaching LLMs your personal taste, and that little gremlin thought entered my head.
Lovely.
Perfect.
Somebody get this man a tiny crown and a plaque that says “About To Waste Three Months.”
I broke down their mechanics, their prose habits, the sentence shapes, the joke shapes, the rhythm, the whole thing.
Then I crammed all of it into one writing skill and expected Claude to become some kind of literary Voltron.
Instead, I built a costume rack.

Claude would reach in, grab a little Kerouac hat, a Sedaris scarf, a Vonnegut lunchbox, and a Thompson jacket soaked in whatever energy drink gets recalled by the FDA, then shuffle onto the stage and go, “Hello.
I am Sean now.”
No, my little demon.
That was the annoying part.
It could break down how someone writes and rebuild the skeleton.
Repetition.
Cadence.
All the little measurable parts.
But writing isn’t only measurable parts.
If it were, every open mic comic with a three-act structure and a dream would be selling out arenas instead of telling jokes to a bartender wiping down the same glass for forty-five minutes.
It was like watching someone do a long jump in slow motion and land directly into a pile of laundry.
The movement was there.
The impact was not.
The Sedaris part was worse because it almost made sense.
Build something up, then kick its ankles out.
Sedaris writes about family a lot, so the model decided that if an essay needed a joke, it should probably land on my mother and sisters.
Small issue.
Unless my parents have been running some kind of long con for three decades, in which case, respect.
That’s commitment.
So I’d be writing about agentic workflows, trying to explain some technical thing, and suddenly the essay would end with a callback to hanging out with my Mom.
Not because the story asked for it.
Just because the model found a pattern and started dragging my imaginary siblings into the room like furniture.
None of it was usable.
It was too elegant in that fake way.
Too polished.
Too convinced it had found the secret door behind my taste when all it had done was put on someone else’s pants and ask me how it looked.
Not great, bud.
Those are not your pants.
I kept tinkering anyway because that’s what you do when a thing is clearly broken but still close enough to make you think the next fix will save it.
Maybe I could hold onto the good parts.
Maybe I could keep the sentence movement, the deflation, the weird little philosophical turns, and toss the rest.
Nope.
About a month or two ago, I finally broke down because I was looking into starting this Substack, and everything coming back made me want to peel my own face off and mail it to myself as a warning.
I'm sorry, but I cannot assist with that request.

findings.sentence: Not just the mechanics—how I string words together, where I put the commas—but the actual soul of it.
The part that makes it sound like me and not like some soulless intern who’s been trained on a thousand strangers’ voices.
So I did what any self-respecting nerd would do: I picked four of my favorite writers—Kerouac, Thompson, Sedaris, Vonnegut—and tried to cram their styles into a single skill.
Sentence length, rhythm, the way they deflate a moment with a joke.
I fed it all in, expecting it to spit out something that sounded like me, just sharper, funnier, more *me*.
What I got instead was a disaster.
The AI leaned hard on Sedaris, which made sense—his whole thing is comedic deflation, the way he turns a mundane moment into something absurd.
And yet, there they were, in every essay, like some kind of AI-generated family drama.
It didn’t *care*.
It just knew Sedaris wrote about his family, so it assumed I did too.
Kerouac was another mess.
The AI nailed the long, flowing sentences—those run-ons that feel like a punch to the face, over and over.
It was just length without the rhythm, like a jazz solo played by someone who’s never heard music.
Thompson, meanwhile, felt like I was ripping lines of blow at 2 a.m.
Which, for the record, I’ve never done.
I added more rules, fed in my own work, scrubbed out the authors one by one.
But it always felt like it was trying too hard to be elegant, like it was performing *writing* instead of just doing it.
And no matter how many adjustments I made, it still didn’t sound like me.
Instead of teaching the AI to mimic my influences, I started grilling it.
It would propose expansions, suggest pivots, but the final decision was always mine.
And slowly, something started to click.
The writing began to sound like me, not because I’d reverse-engineered my style, but because I’d stopped trying to force it.
You start by copying your influences, but eventually, all those voices meld into something that’s only yours.
It’s not about giving it a formula.
It’s about showing it the world through your eyes—your weird, specific, slightly unhinged eyes—and letting it learn from there.
Now, when I write, I don’t just hand the AI a prompt and hope for the best.
I treat it like a creative partner.
I let it push me, challenge me, ask me the questions I haven’t thought to ask myself.
And when it spits out something that sounds like me, I know it’s not because it’s mimicking my style.
Which is more than I can say for some of the essays it used to write about my nonexistent sisters.

findings.sentence: # Four Authors, No Sisters
*I spent three months teaching Claude to write like my heroes.
It handed me a family I don't have.*
I was commuting home on the Staten Island ferry, re-reading Dharma Bums, when I got the idea that cost me three months.

Kerouac does this thing where he keeps a sentence rolling and it punches you in the face, then keeps rolling and punches you again, and by the time it stops the point is lodged somewhere behind your eye.
Around that same stretch I'd found Nate B.
Jones on YouTube, who has a pile of episodes about teaching a model your personal taste.
Those two things shook hands somewhere over the water.
So I built a writing skill.
The plan was that everything after it, my essays, my documents, whatever social post needed to not read like the usual slop, would come out with actual prose behind it.
I picked four.
I researched each one, synthesized how they work, took the style apart down to the moving pieces, and crammed all four into a single skill.
The model understood the assignment perfectly.
Sedaris got the most weight on the essays.
He deflates, and that's how I tend to write, so the machine kept reaching for him any time something needed a joke.
Which is how I started getting punchlines about my mother and my sisters.
I couldn't tell you the exact line anymore.
I'd be writing about agentic workflows, dry technical stuff, and the last beat of the whole thing would swerve into a warm little callback about hanging out with my Mom.
On paper it tracks.
Sedaris writes about his family, so the machine wrote about mine, and wherever mine ran out it just built more.
What doesn't track is family drama wandering into a technical essay and pulling up a chair.
The other three were wrong in their own directions.
The sentence went on and on exactly like I asked and did nothing to anybody.
Here's the part that took me the longest to say out loud.
They did precisely what I told them, every single time, no complaints, no shortcuts.
They can read a writer, break the mechanics down, and hand you the parts in a neat little pile.
What they can't hand you is the thing underneath the parts.
So every output came back competent, foreign, and cringy, and not one line of it sounded like me.
I kept at it anyway, because it kept almost working.
Three months of that.
I was looking into starting a Substack and everything getting sent my way was too cringy to publish and had nothing to do with me or anything I've actually lived.
It was straining to be elegant in every sentence.
First I tried the half measure.
Keep the authors' tendencies, lose the rest, hold onto the good parts.
Very surgical of me.
It still popped up in the worst possible places.
So I deleted all four.
Kept every word I'd written myself, threw out everything they'd given me, and started over.
I brought in the skill chain, piled on more rules, fed the machine my own work, and had Claude write me exercises built to pull out more of me and less of them.
It still poked its head up here and there, which is how I ended up at Alex Lieberman's content machine approach, which is the thing you're reading right now.
A few weeks ago OpenAI quietly stopped ChatGPT from writing in the style of named authors, living or dead.
Legal move, copyright suits.
The sanctioned workaround is that you can describe the techniques all day, you just can't say whose they are.
People are going to be disappointed with what comes out the other side of that.
Not because the workaround fails.
Because no matter how well a model copies somebody's style and welds it onto your work, it won't feel right putting it out there in the world.
I ran the unsanctioned version for three months with the names still attached and it read like a rented tux three sizes off, in every photo, forever.
A model will try to break writing down like a math problem, because that's the only grip it has on the thing.
Mechanics carry you a certain distance in this medium and then they quit on you and go home.
The rest is time, lived experience, and a bunch of sleepless nights spilling your guts onto a keyboard because it has to get out of you or you're not sleeping anyway.
Everybody starts out copying.
But the more you type, the more your influences melt into each other, until what's left is one voice that only you could have come up with.
That's the part you can't hand over as a spec, because it isn't one.
It's residue.
So it doesn't write like anybody now.
It grills me instead.
I brain dump an idea into Claude, invoke /creative-partner, and let it pick through everything I just spewed at it.
It asks questions until the idea stops being a puddle.
It tells me where to expand, where I might want to pivot, and shoves me toward three directions I hadn't considered.
Then it hands the decision back to me.
That's the trade.
It stopped trying to be the writer and became the guy who won't let me leave the room until I say what I actually mean.
Kerouac was never the missing piece.
He was doing just fine on that ferry without my help.

findings.sentence: I Crammed Four Writers Into a Skill Chain and Got an Only Child's Family Drama
Trying to force-feed Claude Kerouac, Sedaris, Thompson, and Vonnegut while learning that mechanics can only get you so far.
I was building a set of prompts for agentic workflows.
The model leaned heavily on David Sedaris for the comedic deflation because it made sense structurally.
The problem was that every joke the machine produced contained a punchline involving my mother and sisters.
What didn't make sense was forcing that domestic subplot into a piece of code architecture.
The model wasn't hallucinating; it was doing exactly as I instructed.
Before the crash, there was the Staten Island ferry.
Jones' YouTube channel, which had episodes about finding ways to teach LLMs personal taste.
So I crammed four authors into a single skill chain: Kerouac, Thompson, Sedaris, and Vonnegut.
I researched and synthesized each one, broke down their mechanics, and tried to force them all in.
For about three months, the model kept trying to be all four writers at once.
Not because the models did a bad job—the output was often technically proficient—but because it was trying too hard to be elegant and the jokes it pulled off were painfully unfunny.
Kerouac gave me the length without the punch-in-the-face effect.
Sedaris kept trying to draft family drama I didn't have.
So I scrapped the authors completely.
Now, instead of trying to clone a ghost writer, I have the model grill me and really dig into the ideas I have.
It becomes my creative partner, pulling things out of me and sparking ideas that weren't there before.
It proposes expansions or where to pivot, but ultimately gives you the final decision after multiple rounds of pushing you in different directions.
You don't inject mechanics; you use the tool to extract the voice you've already built through the grind.
If you're stuck on how to make AI sound like you, stop trying to teach it a ghost writer's habits.
